newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks stricter food safety rules.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks stricter food safety rules.

text.p: The European Commission made a fresh bid on Wednesday to protect consumers better from mad cow disease by urging the removal of risky cattle tissue from food and formally banning exports of British gelatine.
The EU's executive is under pressure to act following a warning from Britain that it may ban imports of beef unless the EU agrees to enforce tough British food safety standards in all member states.
EU inspectors have also criticised most countries for not enforcing rules to eradicate the fatal cattle brain wasting disease, bovine spongiform encepahlopathy (BSE).
"It is prudent to exclude high risk tissues from the food and feed chains," Franz Fischler and Emma Bonino, the EU Farm and Food Safety Commissioners, said in a joint statement.
They added that the EU must urgently adopt a safety first approach towards food production to minimise health risks.
Acting on advice from the World Health Organisation, they resubmitted a proposal to ban the brains, eyes and spinal cord of cattle, sheep and goats over 12 months of age from human and animal food.
The draft proposal will be given a preliminary scrutiny on Friday by senior EU member state veterinary officials who would recommend action for approval either by the Commission or EU farm ministers.
The new rules would apply from October 1, 1997.

In December, 10 EU farm ministers threw out a similar proposal, arguing that it was an unnecessary expense given that their countries were free of BSE and scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease in sheep. Only Britain, Ireland, France, Sweden and Luxembourg backed the move.
The Commission, which argues that no country can be considered totally free of mad cow disease, believes that the situation has changed.
The Netherlands switched position after two cases of BSE were reported there, probably caused by imports of contaminated animal feed.
Other countries are also under pressure.

Germany, France, Spain and Sweden face legal action after criticism in the EU inspectors' reports for failing to implement rules from April 1 requiring meat and bone meal to be processed at higher temperatures and for longer periods.
Infected meat and bone meal mixed into cattle and sheep feed is believed to be the main cause of BSE, which has killed more than 165,000 cattle, mostly in Britain, in the past 10 years.
The Commission's draft proposal also includes a formal ban on British exports of gelatine extracted from British cattle.
However this would only be a cosmetic change as Britain has not been exporting locally sourced gelatine because producers have been unable to meet the strict production standards.
Instead they exported gelatine extracted from imported beef.

The draft proposl also clarifies that beef imported into Britain for processing could be re-exported. Last November the French government closed the Paris branch of the Hard Rock Cafe, a U.S.-style chain organised by the Rank Organisation, alleging that it had imported frozen hamburger from Britain.
